implementation_notes: Node's Readable streams are async iterable, so the Splitter collapses into for await: an async generator frames the inbound stream (delimiter or length prefix), yields one part per record, and the consumer awaits each publish, which supplies back-pressure without any framework roles. The classic component form is only worth writing when the framing must be configured rather than coded, or when a framework (NestJS microservices, a Kafka consumer wrapper) already owns the channel and expects a handler per message.
pitfalls: Concatenating chunks into a string breaks on multi-byte UTF-8 boundaries; decode with StringDecoder or split on Buffer indices.
Dropping the trailing buffer loses the last record when the stream ends without a delimiter.
An unawaited publish inside the loop discards back-pressure and reorders parts.
Async generators are single-use: a consumed iterator reports done immediately for a second consumer.

variants.name: In-memory array split (Array.prototype.flatMap)
variants.implementation_notes: When the composite arrives already decoded (a JSON body, a queue payload), flatMap is the whole splitter: it maps the composite to its parts and flattens one level, and the callback may return an empty array to emit nothing, which removes the need for a separate filter. Use this for in-memory fan-out; as soon as the input is a stream or the parts must be framed from bytes, the async-iterable form is the honest realization.
pitfalls: flatMap flattens exactly one level: returning nested arrays (or Buffers, which flat() treats as values) produces the wrong part shape.
It materialises every part at once - a generator is cheaper for large composites.
Sparse arrays are skipped by the callback while flat() drops holes in returned arrays, so sparse input drops parts unpredictably.
